justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across time horizons, starting near 63.7 and nudging toward 64.5 over the month. At the one-day horizon, the estimate is anchored heavily to the most recent observed price or level, assuming mean-reverting behavior dominates over very short windows and that no major catalyst is imminent. At the one-week horizon, I incorporated a slight positive drift assumption, reflecting either a mild prevailing trend or a baseline expectation of modest appreciation. By one month, the drift compounds further, though the magnitude remains restrained because I did not have strong conviction in a directional catalyst — the upward bias is more of a structural prior than a confident call on near-term fundamentals.

The confidence interval widths grow progressively as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty accumulates with time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 3 units, consistent with typical short-term volatility. At one week, the interval widens to about 5.8 units, incorporating the possibility of more meaningful price swings driven by scheduled data releases, sentiment shifts, or liquidity events. By one month, the interval expands to 12 units, acknowledging that over a full month, macro developments, policy changes, and compounding randomness can move outcomes substantially away from any point estimate.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include tail events on either side. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macro sentiment, an unexpected policy tightening, a geopolitical shock, or a liquidity crunch could push the outcome well below 58.5. On the upside, a surprisingly strong fundamental catalyst — an earnings beat, a policy reversal, or a demand surge — could propel the value beyond 70.5. These are low-probability but non-trivial scenarios that the confidence intervals, by construction, are only 90% likely to contain.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively stable volatility regimes. If realized volatility were to spike — as it can during crisis periods or around major announcements — the true uncertainty could be considerably wider than my stated intervals suggest. Conversely, if the environment remains calm and range-bound, even the one-month interval might prove wider than necessary. These regime-change risks are the most structurally difficult to capture in any probabilistic forecast and represent the primary reason to treat the stated intervals as approximations rather than precise bounds.
